New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani's policies have been criticised by US President Donald Trump, but the two have appeared to have a friendly relationship since Mamdani's election a year ago [File: Adam Gray/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera Staff and APPublished On 1 Nov 20261 Nov 2026
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani says after a phone call with United States President Donald Trump that the mother of a 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was shot dead in the Bronx will be granted a visa.
Mamdani wrote in a post on X on Saturday that he had spoken with Trump about Javits Frimpong, whose mother is seeking to travel to New York to say goodbye to her son.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Zohran Mamdani elected as New York City mayor in historic winlist 2 of 3New York mayor Mamdani sues to block $10,000 teaching aide bonuseslist 3 of 3The murder of Javits Frimpong, a bullied schoolboy in The Bronxend of list
The US president “has agreed to grant her visa immediately”, the mayor wrote.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” he wrote.
There was no immediate comment from Trump.
CCTV footage that captured the last moments of Frimpong’s life showed him being chased by three other teens on Thursday morning as he was on his way to school. He was shot in his abdomen and died the same day in hospital. Thousands of people attended vigils held for the teenager across the city.
The 15-year-old had told his father he was bullied at school. Thomas Frimpong, Javits’s father, called on the police to help him “find justice for my son”. Police have said they are investigating, but no arrests have been made yet.

Bangladesh has formed a new wage board to review the minimum wage for garment workers as it tries to quell a protest movement that has disrupted key industrial hubs.
Despite the announcement on Sunday, thousands of workers demanding higher wages continued protesting around the capital, Dhaka. Clashes were reported with police, who fired tear gas and sound grenades.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Beyond money: Why young Tunisians are considering emigrationlist 2 of 3About 25,000 rally in Madrid in support of Spain’s state pension schemelist 3 of 3What can a global strike of dockworkers achieve for Gaza?end of list
The garment sector is the backbone of Bangladesh’s export-driven economy, employing millions of workers and generating the bulk of the country’s foreign earnings.
Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($242), more than double the current wage of 12,500 taka ($101). They said the rising costs of food, housing, transport and healthcare have sharply eroded their purchasing power.
The six-member board is to include representatives of the government, workers and factory owners and is tasked with determining a new minimum wage.
“The issue of forming the wage board has been resolved. There will be no more problems now,” Ministry of Labour and Employment adviser M Sakhawat Hossain Chowdhury told reporters.
“The workers should return to work and work smoothly,” he added.

item.title: No, France is not ‘burning’
item.description:
By Ludivine BantignyPublished On 1 Nov 20261 Nov 2026Listen
Listen (8 mins)
SaveShare No, France is not ‘burning’ on social mediashare-nodes
Sharefacebook

People take part in a demonstration in Paris, France, on October 31, 2026 [Abdul Saboor/Reuters]
For the past few weeks, images of burning buildings and devastated shopping streets have dominated international media coverage of France. “France is burning”, “France in turmoil”, “Chaos in France”, the headlines have declared, focusing on the violent element of an otherwise peaceful student movement demanding better conditions for education.
To understand why this has happened in the past and is happening today, let us start by examining the word “violence”. In today’s context, it is used indiscriminately to refer to a broken shop window, a police officer injuring a demonstrator, a car set on fire, or shots fired at an unarmed crowd.
This confusion tends to inaccurately place material damage and attacks on people, revolt and its repression, on the same level.
Brazilian archbishop Dom Helder Camara, an advocate of liberation theology, distinguished between three types of violence: the first, that of injustice that oppresses; the second, that of the revolt it provokes; and the third, that of repression.
I would add one more form of violence: that of inequality, discrimination, social humiliation and precarious life. A social order can be violent even in its apparent tranquillity.
French history reminds us how often revolts, the injustices that fuel them and the repressions that answer them are closely intertwined.
The storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, in the lead-up to the outbreak of the French Revolution, is one famous event. It was an act of armed insurrection by revolutionaries who rejected an oppressive absolute monarchy and saw the prison as a symbol of its abuses. Advertisement

Israel’s war on homes
From Hebron to Gaza to southern Lebanon, Israel is tearing down homes, and with them, families' hopes of return.stopStop video(Reuters)By Mohamed HusseinPublished On 1 Nov 20261 Nov 2026

“Around 12:30 at night, the Israeli army vehicles were at al-Jalda Square,” one Hebron resident told Al Jazeera. “They told us to leave our homes. We asked until when, and they said until further notice. We left with the clothes on our backs.”
Hours earlier on October 23, two Israeli soldiers had been killed by armed Palestinian men at a checkpoint near the city. Hebron, the occupied West Bank’s largest city, has been under Israeli siege ever since, with restrictions extending across a governorate of about 800,000 Palestinians.
A black X now marks the homes from which families have been forcibly expelled. Soldiers have moved into others, turning them into military outposts.A black X marks a Palestinian home in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, indicating its residents have been forcibly expelled by Israeli forces [Screen grab/Al Jazeera]
In just over a week, nearly 5,000 Palestinians have been displaced, according to UNRWA, the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, which called the measures collective punishment in violation of international law.
The current operation builds on years of demolitions. From 2009 up until the siege began on October 23, Israeli forces demolished 2,491 buildings and displaced 3,534 Palestinians in the Hebron governorate, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Across Area C and occupied East Jerusalem, the monthly average of demolitions since 2024 has been at least double that of the preceding 15 years.

Anaesthesiologist Manar Fayyad at work before experiencing the psychological trauma that caused him to leave the medical profession [Courtesy of Manar Fayyad/Al Jazeera]By Eyad QatrawiPublished On 1 Nov 20261 Nov 2026
Deir el-Balah, Gaza – Manar Fayyad, 29, an anaesthesiologist at Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, has suffered severe psychological trauma since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.
The turning point came when he discovered that a man lying before him in the operating room was his own brother Shadi, who was killed in an Israeli air strike on December 27, 2023.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Israeli strikes hit Gaza as Health Ministry urges Rafah openinglist 2 of 3Ethnic cleansing fears rise as Israel squeezes space in Gaza: UNlist 3 of 3Education under fire: Gaza’s children face death on their way to schoolend of list
He recalled the moment he was summoned into the operating room to administer anaesthesia to a critically injured man before emergency surgery.
“He died before I could reach him,” he said. “When I arrived in the operating room, I recognised the man’s clothes. I had a strange feeling, so I approached him and uncovered his face. To my shock, he was my brother Shadi, who was 34.”
Since then, the hospital has become inseparable from the traumatic memory, and he has been unable to continue to work, ultimately bringing his professional career to a premature end.
He continues to struggle with the psychological effects of the experience, trying to cope with it on his own without professional help. He has withdrawn from social life and avoids people and noise as he searches for peace since his brother died.

Police have used shields and batons to disperse housing protesters from a tent camp in Portugal’s capital, Lisbon, a week after similar operations drew criticism from protesters and rights groups.
Dozens of officers, some accompanied by police dogs, moved into Rossio Square at about 4:30am (04:30 GMT) on Sunday, a day after thousands marched demanding the government withdraw a rental bill they say would deepen the country’s housing crisis.

Protesters had erected more than 50 tents following Saturday’s march through Lisbon. Police commander Iuri Rodrigues issued three warnings to remove the tents, saying they had been erected illegally and that anyone resisting their removal could face disobedience charges.
Hundreds of demonstrators shielding the camp were dispersed, while police also dismantled a smaller encampment in Porto’s Dom Joao I square.
Earlier, lawmaker Pedro Delgado Alves said Rossio Square was peaceful and that nothing justified “a police intervention involving force, physical violence or baton charges, the kind of scenes we witnessed last week”.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi meets with Oman's Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi in Tehran on August 25, 2026. [Handout/Iranian Foreign Ministry, WANA via Reuters]
Proposing a non-aggression pact amid regional hostilities may seem premature. Yet agreements to stop war matter most when distrust is the deepest. The key question is whether regional governments can agree on rules that make their disagreements less destructive.
In a recent lecture at Cambridge University in the UK, Oman’s Foreign Minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, called for a non-aggression pact among all eight Gulf littoral states: the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council along with Iraq and Iran. He described it as the essential prerequisite for an inclusive regional security architecture.
Could such a pact work? As Albusaidi conceded, it would be hard to achieve. But as another major escalation looms between Iran and the United States, the region urgently needs a diplomatic path forward.
Indeed, the ongoing conflict has proved so hard to resolve because the region’s security arrangements have remained underdeveloped, relying for too long on external powers. The way forward then can be an inclusive agreement.
Reviving the promise of 1976
The Omani proposal is anchored in a historic precedent. In November 1976, the foreign ministers of all eight Gulf littoral states met in Muscat to pursue collective security after Britain’s withdrawal from the region.
It remains the only time all eight have sat at one table. The Iranian Revolution, the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the Iran–Iraq war then pushed the region towards defensive arrangements that later hardened into exclusion. Advertisement

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says President Donald Trump’s administration did not help Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro flee the country for the United States after losing a run-off to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Bolsonaro arrived in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday, a day after the US Department of State said Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas after his October 25 election loss, which bucked a trend of conservative electoral wins in Latin America.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3What’s next for Brazil’s Flavio Bolsonaro after election defeat?list 2 of 3Trump says won’t ‘take sides’ in Brazil election, but calls it a ‘disgrace’list 3 of 3Brazil summons Argentinian diplomat over Bolsonaro’s flight to USend of list
Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion, and before leaving, he had been ordered to surrender his passport because police deemed him a flight risk.
“We didn’t facilitate anything,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday in Atlanta, Georgia, where diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies were gathered.
“We had word that he had arrived in the United States. He had previously held a visa, and the president made a decision to allow him to enter the country,” Rubio said.
He added that the US government was not “involved directly in any of the moves that were made”.
